components.gap: Supply the full Feller II.9 treatment of Stirling's formula with the constant and Robbins bounds (Feller, Volume I, third edition, pp. 52-54 and the VII.2 constant passage, pp. 179-181). Missing on the route: (i) the historical attributions of II.9: the formula is James Stirling's, Methodus differentialis, 1730 (p. 52, note 14); the d_n argument and inequality (9.14) are due to H. E. Robbins, Amer. Math. Monthly 62 (1955), pp. 26-29 (p. 53, note 15; the route only names Robbins in titles and the index, without attributing the argument or giving the reference); the usual proof that e^C = sqrt(2 pi) relies on Wallis's formula, and Feller gives a direct proof in Amer. Math. Monthly (1967) (p. 53, note 16). (ii) Feller's justificatory claims: Stirling's formula as an important tool of analytical probability, invaluable for theory and for numerical approximation (p. 52); the choice of d_n by comparing log n! with a quantity near the arithmetic mean of the extreme members of (9.5) (pp. 52-53); the proof that e^C = sqrt(2 pi) is elementary, independent of chapters IV-VI, and postponed to VII.2 because it is naturally connected with the normal approximation theorem (p. 53). (iii) The accuracy statement for (9.15) on p. 54: the double inequality supplements Stirling's formula remarkably; the ratio of its extreme members is close to 1 - (12n^2)^(-1), so the right-hand member overestimates n! with an error of less than a stated multiple of n^(-2) per cent, and in reality much less. (iv) Narrowed variant: Feller states the VII.2 central-ratio relation (2.5)/(2.7) for 0 < k < K_nu with K_nu^3/nu^2 to 0 and error below k^3/nu^2 (pp. 180-181); the route proves it only for k <= M sqrt(n) (annex 188-207).

components.gap: Supply Feller's numerical approximations from II.9 (Feller, Volume I, third edition): the right side of (9.1) approximates 1! by 0.9221 and 2! by 1.919 (and 5! by 118.019), with percentage errors 8, 4 and 2; 10! = 3,628,800 is approximated by 3,598,600 with an error of 0.8 per cent; for 100! the error is 0.08 per cent; the approximation is remarkably accurate even for small n (p. 52); and the values of the right-hand member of (9.15): 2.0007 for n = 2 and 120.01 for n = 5 (p. 54). The route gives only the n = 5 values (118.019 and the computed 120.003, body 319-321), without the other examples, the percentage errors, the n = 2 value or Feller's printed 120.01.
